sentences: The problem is when the role takes over the relationship.
She can be my little girl sometimes without becoming my child.
She still has to remain responsible for her life and keep reparenting herself.
It can run the other way too.
I make her Mom when I expect her to regulate me, soothe every wound, organize my life, and keep me functional.

haiku: The two paragraphs mirror each other closely, with the second opening as a deliberate counterpart to the first and both closing on a neat clause or list, and the sentence lengths stay evenly matched. That balance reads as built rather than spoken, though the first-person voice and concrete domestic detail keep the machine signal mostly in the architecture and the stock phrasings rather than in the diction as a whole. These are style features only and do not establish authorship.
sonnet: The paragraph is built as two mirror-image halves (role takes over one way, then "the other way too"), each a short claim followed by a list or rule, and that symmetry is more systematic than lived. Every sentence is a general statement with no scene, detail, or specific incident, so the voice sounds like advice being organized rather than someone remembering.
